cards: Timur, also known as Tamerlane, was a Turco-Mongol conqueror who rose to power in Transoxiana in the late fourteenth century and founded the Timurid Empire.
Dante Alighieri was a Florentine poet and politician, author of the Divine Comedy.
Alauddin Khalji was a sultan of the Delhi Sultanate who reigned from 1296 until his death in 1316.
Ibn Khaldun was an Arab historian and thinker born in Tunis in 1332 to a family of Andalusi origin.
Petrarch, Francesco Petrarca, was an Italian poet and scholar born in Arezzo in 1304.
The Hongwu Emperor, born Zhu Yuanzhang, was a peasant-born rebel leader who founded the Ming dynasty in 1368.
Muhammad bin Tughluq was sultan of Delhi from 1325 to 1351.
Bayezid I was an Ottoman sultan of the late fourteenth century, known for rapid conquests in the Balkans and Anatolia.
Amda Seyon I was emperor of Ethiopia who acceded in 1314.
Dmitry Donskoy was Grand Prince of Moscow from 1359 and of Vladimir from 1362.
Louis IV, called the Bavarian, was a Wittelsbach duke elected King of Germany in 1314 and crowned emperor in Rome in 1328 without papal consent.
Valdemar IV, known as Valdemar Atterdag, was King of Denmark from 1340 to 1375 and rebuilt the kingdom after years in which its provinces had been pawned to foreign lords, recovering Zealand, Scania…
Algirdas was grand duke of Lithuania from 1345 to 1377.
Edward III of England reigned from 1327 to 1377.
Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375) was an Italian writer and humanist, born in or near Florence, who spent his youth in Naples in the circle of the court of King Robert of Anjou.
Tokhtamysh (died 1406) was a Mongol khan descended from Jochi who, with the support of Timur, became khan of the White Horde and by 1380 reunited it with the Golden Horde.
Ivan I Danilovich, called Kalita ('moneybag'), was Prince of Moscow from 1325 and Grand Prince of Vladimir from 1328 until his death in 1340.
Louis I of Hungary, known as Louis the Great, was king of Hungary and Croatia from 1342 and king of Poland from 1370 until his death in 1382.
Margaret I was the ruler of Denmark, Norway and Sweden.
Philip the Bold was the youngest son of John II of France, who granted him the Duchy of Burgundy in 1363.
Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan was the last effective ruler of the Ilkhanate, the Mongol state centred on Iran.
Charles I of Hungary, also called Charles Robert, was the first Angevin king of Hungary, who won the throne after the Árpád line died out in 1301.
Gian Galeazzo Visconti ruled part of the Milanese lands from 1378, seized sole power from his uncle Bernabò in 1385 and in 1395 bought from King Wenceslaus the title of Duke of Milan.
Hafez was a Persian poet of Shiraz, the most celebrated master of the ghazal, or lyric love poem.
Peter IV, called the Ceremonious, was king of Aragon from 1336.
Edigu was an emir of the Mangit tribe who, though not a descendant of Genghis Khan, dominated the Golden Horde from about 1396 to 1411 through puppet khans.
Firuz Shah Tughluq was Sultan of Delhi from 1351 to 1388.
Al-Nasir Muhammad was a sultan of the Mamluk Sultanate whose main reign lasted from 1310 to 1341.
Ramathibodi I, known before his accession as U Thong, was the founder and first king of Ayutthaya, ruling from 1351 to 1369.
Rupert of the Palatinate was Elector Palatine and King of the Romans from 1400, when the electors deposed Wenceslaus, until his death in 1410.
Azzone Visconti was lord of Milan from 1329 to 1339.
Coluccio Salutati (1331–1406) was an Italian humanist and chancellor of the Republic of Florence from 1375 until his death.
Edward II was king of England from 1307 to 1327, the son of Edward I.
Edward the Black Prince (Edward of Woodstock) was the eldest son of Edward III of England and a celebrated commander of the Hundred Years' War.
Gediminas was Grand Duke of Lithuania from about 1316 until his death and founder of the Gediminid dynasty.
Jan Hus was a Czech priest and reformer, rector of the University of Prague, whose criticism of church abuses drew on the ideas of John Wycliffe.
John II, called the Good, was King of France from 1350 to 1364, during the Hundred Years' War.
John of Luxembourg, known as John the Blind, was King of Bohemia from 1310 to 1346.
Manuel Chrysoloras was a Byzantine scholar and diplomat who taught Greek in Florence from 1397, the first sustained teaching of the language in Italy for centuries.
Raden Wijaya was the founder and first ruler of the Majapahit Empire in eastern Java, reigning from 1293 to 1309 CE.
